candidate.claim: Zero repulsion, class-number formulas, nonvanishing proportions, close-gap thresholds, and forced high-order central zeros show that progress on one L-function can arise from controlling an entire family rather than studying it in isolation.
candidate.proposed_limit: The proposed family moment and exponential-sum estimates remain unproved and even the more elaborate program described would initially yield only a quasi-RH zero-free line.

parents.title: A hypothetical exceptional zero forces repulsion and class-number growth elsewhere

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Dirichlet's class-number formula links arithmetic classes to L(1,chi_d), so excluding a real zero near one would make class-number lower bounds effective. Conversely, a hypothetical near-one zero for one character conditionally strengthens bounds for other discriminants and repels comparable zeros elsewhere; the source's small-prime Möbius-mimicry discussion is an intuition for this family-wide interaction, not a complete derivation of repulsion. The same span gives two conditional elimination routes: any fixed improvement below the Brun–Titchmarsh constant two, or ruling out the stated alternative normalized-gap hypothesis, would eliminate the exceptional zero.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: It traces one obstruction through several representations and distinguishes a heuristic local explanation from the explicit conditional mechanisms that would remove it.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted after revision because it removes an imported theorem label, qualifies the mimicry explanation, and restores the two mechanisms the critic found missing.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The span contains the class-number formula, conditional effects of a near-one real zero, Siegel ineffectivity, the small-prime character analogy, and both Brun–Titchmarsh and gap-based implications. Exact constants and exponents are scan-sensitive.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The Landau–Siegel zero is hypothetical; Möbius mimicry is source intuition, while the proposed inequality and gap improvements are conditional routes, not achievements.

parents.title: Three routes hit sharp thresholds just before eliminating the exceptional zero

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Three mathematically different observables meet the same implication-changing threshold: improving the Brun–Titchmarsh constant below two, proving a normalized neighbor gap strictly below one half, or exceeding fifty percent nonvanishing in the modular family would each eliminate the Landau–Siegel zero. Comparing the thresholds shows how substantial partial control can still miss the one margin that changes the conclusion. These are barriers of the reported methods, not impossibility theorems for future refinements.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: It aligns three unlike methods by the exact point at which each would change the exceptional-zero implication, without collapsing their mechanisms.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted because the cross-method threshold comparison is source-grounded, non-generic, and preserves the critic's non-absoluteness qualification.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The source explicitly states all three conditional thresholds and reports the achieved near-threshold results. Constants and the normalized-gap display are formula-sensitive because the columns interleave.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: Predicted behavior beyond the thresholds is conjectural; the stated current barriers are method-specific assessments.

parents.title: Forced multiple central zeros convert exotic L-functions into effective arithmetic bounds

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Goldfeld's move is to amplify a borderline central-zero signal by multiplicity: a simple central zero barely misses a growing class-number bound, while higher-order vanishing supplies enough quantitative leverage. Gross–Zagier triple-zero examples yield an effective logarithmic-power lower bound and solve class-number divergence, though the result remains far below the expected power scale. High-rank elliptic-curve L-functions are the conjecturally motivated place to seek such extremal vanishing, not a proved general rank-to-multiplicity bridge in this span.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: It identifies multiplicity as an amplification mechanism and compares the exact strength gained with the much stronger scale still missing.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted because it performs a concrete signal-amplification analysis while retaining the achieved bound, its weakness, and the conjectural bridge.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The source contrasts simple and multiple central zeros, reports Goldfeld's observation and Gross–Zagier examples, and states the effective but weak class-number bound. The high-rank motivation is explicitly tied to Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer belief; the epsilon glyph is damaged.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The achieved triple-zero consequence is reported as proved; systematic high-rank/central-multiplicity expectations are conjectural.

parents.title: Iwaniec proposes approximating Möbius with coefficients from a forced-vanishing family

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Iwaniec proposes replacing the difficult Möbius coefficients by linear combinations from an engineered elliptic-curve L-function family with forced multiple central vanishing. That structured family is intended to carry both cancellation and multiplicity, relocating the obstruction into a family second-moment estimate, uniform square-root cancellation for an incomplete exponential sum, and the stated system of conjectures. Elimination of the Landau–Siegel zero remains conditional, and similar more complicated conditional constructions would yield only a fixed zero-free line short of RH.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: It decomposes the proposed bridge into the properties engineered into the auxiliary family and the distinct conjectural estimates where the original difficulty reappears.
